findings.title: KeyError crash when existing Integration has no 'sender' in metadata
findings.body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the new user-verification check does `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. Integration.metadata is a schemaless JSON field, and `build_integration` only writes `metadata["sender"]` when the pipeline state contains a sender (`if state.get("sender")`). Integration rows created before sender tracking existed, or created through any flow where the sender was never bound into pipeline state, will not have this key. When such an ACTIVE Integration exists without an OrganizationIntegration (exactly the branch this check runs in, e.g. re-linking after an uninstall), the check raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of the intended 'Invalid installation request' page, permanently blocking that installation flow. This should use a defensive lookup such as `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat a missing sender as a verification failure (rendering the error page) rather than crashing.

findings.title: OAuth token exchange and /user lookup are not wrapped in error handling
findings.body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` (line 423) and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (line 434) are called without any exception handling. Only the reading/decoding of the response body is wrapped in try/except. If GitHub is unreachable, times out, or returns a 5xx, safe_urlopen raises; if the freshly issued token is rejected, get_user_info raises ApiError. In all of these transient-failure cases the user gets an unhandled 500 rather than the friendly 'We could not verify the authenticity of the installation request' page that this PR explicitly designs for every other failure mode (bad state, missing access_token, missing login). These calls should be wrapped so network/API failures render the same error response.

findings.title: redirect_uri omitted from the OAuth token exchange even though it was sent in the authorize request
findings.body: OAuthLoginView builds the token-exchange payload with only code, client_id, and client_secret, but the authorize redirect a few lines above includes a `redirect_uri` parameter. RFC 6749 §4.1.3 requires that redirect_uri be included (and identical) in the token request when it was present in the authorization request, and the code comments claim this mirrors `OAuth2CallbackView.get_token_params` / `exchange_token`, which do include redirect_uri. If GitHub enforces this (it does for mismatch cases), the exchange returns an error payload with no access_token and every GitHub installation fails at this step. The test suite stubs the token endpoint without validating the request body, so it would not catch this. Add `redirect_uri` (the same absolute_uri value used in the authorize URL) to the POST data.

findings.title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the installation-not-found path
findings.body: test_installation_not_found still stubs a 404 for GET /app/installations/{id} and is named for that scenario, but it now completes the OAuth step with a deliberately wrong `state` value (`ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`, which does not match the pipeline signature `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` used everywhere else). The request therefore fails at the state check in OAuthLoginView, before GitHubInstallation or build_integration ever run, so the stubbed 404 is never hit and the assertion on the generic 'Invalid installation request.' message would pass regardless. The 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' branch in build_integration (ApiError 404 -> IntegrationError) is now uncovered. The test should either be renamed to reflect that it tests state mismatch, or reworked to pass the correct state so it actually exercises the 404 path again.
